title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Greenville, SC | Genstone
metaDescription: Greenville, SC investor renovations: mill village houses, North Main bungalows and Upstate ranches priced free before you buy, with draws paid as work is done.
intro: Greenville once called itself the textile center of the world, and the mill villages ringing its west side are now some of the most active renovation territory in the Upstate. Judson, Monaghan, Poe, Dunean and Brandon still hold rows of company-built houses on brick piers, while North Main and Augusta Road carry the bungalows and revival houses of the city's early professional class, and post-war ranches spread out toward Berea, Taylors and Mauldin. A downtown that has grown into a regional destination, plus employers like BMW, Michelin and Prisma Health, keep demand for all of it strong. Genstone Construction renovates those houses for investors, lenders and servicers across Greenville County, working from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters through vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors and a designated field manager on each project. Every job starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that prices the work and checks the after-repair value before you commit, followed by an itemized scope with draws paid against completed work, no upfront payment and a one-year workmanship warranty after you approve the house.
housingStock:
Greenville's mill villages are its most distinctive investor inventory. Textile companies built Judson, Monaghan, Poe, Dunean, Brandon, Woodside, Mills Mill and others in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, often laying out whole neighborhoods of nearly identical one-story and story-and-a-half frame houses around the mill. Typical features include brick pier foundations over shallow crawlspaces, heart pine floors, board or plaster walls covered by later materials, central chimneys, small rooms and rear additions built over many decades. Many of the mills have closed or been converted, and several villages sit outside the city limits in unincorporated Greenville County.

Closer to downtown, North Main, Hampton-Pinckney, Pettigru, East Park, Colonel Elias Earle and the Augusta Road area, including Alta Vista, hold Victorian houses, Craftsman bungalows and period revival homes from the 1890s through the 1940s. These are often larger houses on raised crawlspaces or partial basements, with plaster walls, original millwork and deep porches on sloping lots. Nicholtown, Southernside and other east and west side neighborhoods have early twentieth-century houses alongside later infill.

After World War II, Greenville spread outward with brick ranches in Overbrook, Sans Souci, Berea, Taylors, Wade Hampton and the areas along Laurens and Pleasantburg roads, many on crawlspaces with some basements on hillside lots. Suburban growth since the 1980s has filled Mauldin, Simpsonville, Greer and Five Forks with subdivisions of brick and vinyl houses.

For investors, each era leads to a predictable budget. Mill houses spend on piers, floor framing, termite damage, complete wiring and plumbing, insulation and a second bathroom. Older downtown-area houses spend on plaster, wiring, plumbing, windows and historic overlay requirements. Ranches spend on HVAC, electrical service, kitchens, baths and crawlspace moisture. Suburban houses mainly need roofs, HVAC, water heaters and windows as original components wear out together.

commonIssues.title: Settled piers and sagging floors in mill houses
commonIssues.body: Greenville's mill houses were built on brick piers that often rest on shallow footings in red clay. A century of moisture, missing mortar and soil movement leaves piers leaning or sunk and floors sloping, sometimes dramatically. Long joist spans and old notching make it worse. Correcting the foundation means rebuilding or re-setting piers on proper footings, adding beams and sistering damaged joists before any finish work starts. We look under the house during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review because this work varies widely in cost.

commonIssues.title: Red clay drainage and crawlspace moisture
commonIssues.body: The Upstate's red clay holds water and drains slowly, and hillside lots send runoff straight toward foundations. Crawlspaces under mill houses, bungalows and ranches stay damp, leading to rotted sills, mold on framing, sagging insulation and rusted ductwork. Partial basements on sloping lots take on water after heavy storms. The fix usually starts outside with grading, gutters and downspout extensions, then adds vapor barriers, drainage and sometimes encapsulation or dehumidification depending on the exit strategy.

commonIssues.title: Termite damage
commonIssues.body: Subterranean termites are active throughout the Upstate, and older houses with wood close to damp soil are especially vulnerable. Damage turns up in sills, joists, door frames, porch framing and the bottoms of wall studs. Most lenders require a clean CL-100 wood infestation report before closing, so a Greenville rehab budget should include treatment and repair of damaged framing, along with correcting the grading, gutter and wood-to-soil conditions that invited termites in the first place.

commonIssues.title: Original wiring and plumbing
commonIssues.body: Mill houses and older downtown-area houses often contain knob-and-tube wiring, ungrounded circuits, undersized electrical service, galvanized supply lines and cast-iron or clay drains, and some later houses have polybutylene supply pipe. Insurers and buyer inspectors flag these systems quickly. A Greenville rehab of any pre-1950 house should generally assume full electrical replacement with a new panel and service, a PEX repipe and a camera inspection of the sewer lateral, since roots and broken clay pipe are common under mature trees.

commonIssues.title: Ice storm damage and older roofs
commonIssues.body: The Upstate gets more ice and snow than the rest of South Carolina, and ice storms bring down limbs and trees on roofs, porches and power lines. Older roofs in mill villages and established neighborhoods often show past storm damage, patched decking and failing flashing around chimneys. A Greenville scope should include roof and decking evaluation, chimney flashing and crown repair, and a look at large trees near the house, since removal or trimming may be needed before the new roof goes on.

investorMarket:
Greenville's investor market has been shaped by the rebirth of its downtown and the Swamp Rabbit Trail, which runs past several mill villages on its way to Travelers Rest. Judson, Poe, Monaghan and other villages near the trail and the Village of West Greenville arts district have seen rapid renovation, and flips there sell to buyers who want character, walkability and proximity to downtown. North Main, Augusta Road, Alta Vista and the historic overlay neighborhoods attract buyers looking for larger older houses and pay well for careful renovations.

Rental and BRRRR investors tend to focus on post-war ranches in Berea, Taylors, Wade Hampton, Parker and the areas along Laurens and White Horse roads, along with some mill villages where renovation hasn't yet pushed prices up. Employers such as BMW in Greer, Michelin, Prisma Health and a large base of manufacturers and distribution companies keep rental demand steady. Furman University and Bob Jones University support some student and staff rentals, and Clemson is close enough to influence parts of the market to the west.

Small multifamily includes duplexes scattered through older neighborhoods, divided houses near downtown, and 1960s through 1980s duplexes and fourplexes in the suburbs. REO properties appear across the county, often in older houses with structural or systems issues.
permits:
The City of Greenville's building codes staff issue building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits and perform inspections for properties inside the city limits. Several of the mill villages and many suburban areas are in unincorporated Greenville County, where the county's building safety office handles permits, and Mauldin, Simpsonville, Greer, Travelers Rest and other towns run their own departments. Confirming the jurisdiction is an early step on any Greenville project. Permits are needed for structural repairs, pier and foundation work, wall removals, additions, new or relocated plumbing and electrical, HVAC replacements, water heaters, roofing beyond minor repairs and decks. South Carolina applies statewide building codes, and residential contractors must be licensed or registered through the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission.

The city's preservation overlay districts, including Hampton-Pinckney, Pettigru, East Park and Colonel Elias Earle, require design review for exterior changes such as window replacement, porch work, siding, additions and demolition. Genstone's field manager confirms the jurisdiction, handles permit applications and design review, schedules inspections and collects lien waivers from every trade.
climate: Greenville's climate is humid subtropical, but its Upstate location near the Blue Ridge foothills brings cooler winters and more frequent ice and snow than the Midlands or the coast. Ice storms are the main winter hazard, bringing limbs down on roofs, knocking out power to vacant houses and freezing exposed plumbing. Summers are hot and humid, which loads air conditioners and keeps crawlspaces damp, and summer thunderstorms test gutters, grading and basement drainage on hilly lots. Remnants of tropical systems occasionally bring heavy rain and wind inland, as Helene did in 2024. For scheduling, roofing, siding and exterior paint are easiest to schedule in spring and fall. Winter work on vacant houses requires freeze protection, and summer work favors interior projects in conditioned space.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have a Greenville office?
faqs.a: No. Genstone's headquarters, and its only office, is in Romeoville, Illinois. In Greenville and across the Upstate we work through a network of vetted, licensed and insured South Carolina contractors, and each project has a designated Genstone field manager who oversees scope, schedule, permits and inspections. Photos and milestones are shared throughout, which helps investors from outside the area, as well as lenders and institutional owners, manage Greenville renovations without regular site visits.

faqs.a: On Greenville houses we focus on pier and floor framing condition, crawlspace and basement moisture, termite damage and the likely CL-100 outcome, wiring and plumbing age, roof and tree condition, and whether the property is inside the city, in unincorporated Greenville County or in a preservation overlay district. We estimate the repair cost, compare the after-repair value with nearby sales and tell you whether the numbers support your offer.

faqs.a: Yes. Our Greenville-area work covers the Upstate, including Mauldin, Simpsonville, Greer, Taylors, Travelers Rest, Easley, Berea and Fountain Inn. Each jurisdiction has its own permitting office and zoning rules, and we work with the correct one for each property. Our process doesn't change: free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, line-item estimate with a draw schedule, a designated field manager and payment tied to completed work.

faqs.q: How do payments work on a Greenville project?
faqs.a: You don't pay anything before work begins. The estimate lays out the draws, and each one is paid once its stage is finished, photographed and, where required, inspected. We hold the final invoice until the work is complete and you've accepted it. Debris hauling is already in the price, and a one-year workmanship warranty follows, excluding tenant damage and normal wear.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Greenville, SC | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip contractor in Greenville, SC: mill village houses near the Swamp Rabbit Trail, North Main bungalows and Upstate ranches scoped to local comps.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Greenville
fix-flip.intro: Greenville's mill villages have become some of the most rewarding flip territory in the Upstate, but only for investors who price the structure correctly. A Judson or Poe mill house can look like a cosmetic project from the street and turn out to need new piers, new floor framing, complete wiring and plumbing and termite repair. Meanwhile, buyers on North Main and Augusta Road expect careful renovations that respect older houses, and buyers in suburban neighborhoods compare flips with new construction. Genstone Construction scopes Greenville flips against nearby renovated sales and prices the hidden items first. Our estimates are itemized, include a draw schedule and often compare two finish levels with separate after-repair values. A designated field manager runs each project with licensed South Carolina trades.

sections.h2: Mill villages along the Swamp Rabbit Trail
sections.body:
Judson, Poe, Monaghan and the other villages near the Swamp Rabbit Trail and the Village of West Greenville sell to buyers who want to live near downtown, the trail and the restaurants and studios that have grown up around them. Many are young professionals and first-time buyers, and they compare your flip against renovated mill houses on the same street. Those buyers want original heart pine floors refinished, porches restored, and a floor plan that works in a small footprint, which often means opening the kitchen, adding a second bathroom and finding space for laundry.

The structure comes first. Most mill houses need pier rebuilding, beam and joist repair and termite damage correction. Wiring and plumbing are typically replaced entirely, and insulation and air sealing make a big difference in comfort and utility bills. Because several villages sit outside city limits, permits often go through Greenville County rather than the city. We price the structural work up front so it doesn't surprise you after demolition, and we set the finish level to match the strongest renovated sales nearby.

sections.h2: North Main, Augusta Road and the overlay districts
sections.body:
North Main, Augusta Road, Alta Vista and the historic overlay neighborhoods of Hampton-Pinckney, Pettigru, East Park and Colonel Elias Earle attract buyers who want larger older houses close to downtown. They expect a renovation that preserves original millwork, floors and porches while delivering modern systems, kitchens and baths. Plaster is often repaired rather than removed, and windows are restored or carefully replaced.

In the preservation overlay districts, exterior changes need design review, which affects windows, porches, siding and additions. We prepare those submissions early and design exterior work to fit the guidelines. Behind the walls, these houses typically need rewiring, a new panel, PEX supply lines, a camera-inspected sewer lateral, HVAC sized for older floor plans and crawlspace or basement drainage. Finish levels should match the strongest renovated sales nearby, which in these neighborhoods means quality materials and careful detail. We price options against comps so you can match the scope to the street.

sections.h2: Upstate inspections and Greenville flip closings
sections.body:
Most Greenville flips that run into trouble under contract do so because of the CL-100 termite report or the home inspection. Lenders typically require a clean CL-100, and inspectors look closely at foundations and floor framing, crawlspace moisture, roof condition, electrical safety and HVAC performance.

We address those items before finishes. That means termite treatment and framing repair with documentation, pier and floor corrections, crawlspace vapor barriers and drainage, a panel upgrade and rewiring, a new roof with proper decking and flashing and an HVAC system sized for the house. Exterior work is scheduled for spring and fall when possible, and vacant houses are protected against freezing during winter ice storms. Each draw waits for completed work, and photos and inspection results reach you as they happen. For financing, Genstone Financial has fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, and any outside lender works too. The permit and inspection records become part of the package your listing agent shares with buyers.

faqs.q: Are Greenville mill houses good flips?
faqs.a: They can be, especially in villages where renovated houses nearby have set a strong resale price. What sinks mill house flips is a light foundation budget, because piers, sills and joists so often need work. We crawl under the house during the free review, so the structural number is real before you sign. After the structure is fixed, the small square footage keeps finishes affordable.

faqs.q: Is my Greenville property in the city or the county?
faqs.a: Many mill villages and suburban areas around Greenville are in unincorporated Greenville County, even though they have Greenville addresses. That affects which office issues permits and which zoning rules apply. We confirm the jurisdiction during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and handle permits through the correct office for each property. Annexation over the years has left a patchwork, so two houses a few blocks apart in the same mill village can fall under different offices. Getting it right before you file avoids a rejected application and a lost week.

faqs.q: Do you handle flips in Greer, Mauldin and Simpsonville?
faqs.a: Yes. We work across Greenville County and nearby areas, including Greer, Mauldin, Simpsonville, Taylors and Travelers Rest. Suburban flips typically involve newer construction with fewer structural issues, so the focus shifts to roofs, HVAC, kitchens, baths and flooring, and buyers often compare your flip against new construction nearby. In the Five Forks area and around Greer near the BMW plant, buyers tend to be relocating professionals who expect updated kitchens and baths at a level close to new construction.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Greenville, SC | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovations in Greenville, SC: Upstate ranches and mill houses rehabbed to appraise and rent, supported by BMW, Michelin and regional employers.
brrrr.intro: Greenville's growth has pushed purchase prices up in its most popular neighborhoods, but the Upstate still offers BRRRR opportunities in post-war ranch neighborhoods and less-discovered mill villages. Rental demand is supported by a broad base of employers, including BMW, Michelin, Prisma Health and hundreds of manufacturers and distribution companies. Genstone Construction renovates BRRRR properties across Greenville County to reach the refinance appraisal and hold up to years of tenants. Our estimators build scopes from nearby renovated sales, a designated field manager runs each job with licensed South Carolina trades, and every repair is documented for your refinance lender and appraiser. Mill houses and ranches here often hide pier, termite and moisture problems under fresh paint, so we price those before you close rather than after demolition.

sections.body:
Upstate BRRRR projects tend to start where prices are still moderate and renters are plentiful. Berea, Parker, Taylors, Wade Hampton and the neighborhoods along Laurens, White Horse and Poinsett highways have large inventories of post-war ranches and smaller houses that fit the model. Some mill villages farther from the Swamp Rabbit Trail, where renovation hasn't yet pushed prices up, also work. Nearby towns such as Easley, Greer and Fountain Inn offer more options.

Every Greenville candidate should go through the free review first. We price the complete rehab, line it up against renovated sales on nearby Upstate streets and show you whether the refinance should hand your capital back. Greenville-specific risks include pier and framing damage in mill houses, termite damage, crawlspace moisture, sewer laterals damaged by roots and ice-storm damage to roofs. Those can still be good buys, but only when the costs are known before closing. Houses within a reasonable drive of the BMW plant in Greer or the Michelin facilities tend to draw steady applicants.

sections.h2: Renovating for the Greenville refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers in Greenville County compare your rental against renovated sales and rate its condition and quality. A house with a renovated kitchen and baths, new flooring, a newer heat pump, an updated electrical panel and a recent roof earns a stronger rating than one with partial updates. Visible issues such as sloping floors, water stains, termite damage or an old panel can pull the rating down.

Greenville scopes are written to remove each of those markdowns. For Greenville ranches, that usually includes HVAC replacement with sealed ductwork, roof replacement when needed, a panel upgrade, PEX supply lines, crawlspace vapor barrier and drainage, termite treatment and repair, kitchen and bath renovation and durable flooring. Mill houses add pier and framing work. We provide an appraisal package with permit records, final inspections, the CL-100, an improvement list and before-and-after photos so the appraiser has documented evidence of the work. Where a ranch on a hillside lot has a partial basement, we also make sure the space is dry before the appraiser sees it, since water staining below grade lowers the condition rating quickly.

sections.h2: Materials for Upstate summers and winters
sections.body:
A Greenville rental has to handle hot, humid summers and winters with occasional ice and hard freezes. HVAC comes first: a properly sized heat pump with sealed ducts keeps tenants comfortable in both seasons and reduces service calls. Insulating supply lines in crawlspaces and basements protects against freezing during ice storms, which matters most if the house sits vacant between tenants.

Inside, luxury vinyl plank handles moisture and pets, and refinished hardwood works in older ranches and mill houses where the floors are sound. Bathrooms get outdoor-vented fans and tub walls without grout joints to fail. Under the house, vapor barriers and drainage corrections reduce moisture. Outside, gutters, downspout extensions and grading keep water away from the foundation and make the house less attractive to termites. A renewable termite bond protects framing over time. These choices reduce work orders and support the next refinance or eventual sale. Heat pumps in the Upstate also need proper auxiliary heat for the coldest nights, which reduces no-heat calls during ice storms.

faqs.q: Do manufacturing employers affect Greenville rental demand?
faqs.a: They're a large part of it. BMW, Michelin and many other manufacturers and suppliers employ large workforces in the Upstate, and many of those workers rent. We don't predict rents or occupancy, but well-renovated houses with reasonable commutes to major employers generally compete well in the Greenville rental market. Many of those tenants are transferees and new hires who lease before they arrive, so clear listing photos and documented upgrades help a Greenville rental stand out. Shift workers also tend to value quiet bedrooms and reliable air conditioning.

faqs.q: Can a mill house work as a BRRRR in Greenville?
faqs.a: Yes, if the purchase price leaves room for the structural and systems work most mill houses need and renovated comps nearby support the refinance. The risk is underestimating piers, framing and termite repair. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks under the house before you buy so those costs are included in your numbers. Villages farther from the trail, such as parts of Brandon, Dunean and Mills Mill, sometimes leave more room between purchase and appraised value than the most popular ones.

faqs.q: Can Genstone coordinate the DSCR refinance?
faqs.a: Through Genstone Financial, the Genstone Companies offer DSCR rental loans along with fix-and-flip loans and credit lines. Using them is optional. With any lender, we provide the itemized scope, permit records, inspection results, CL-100 and photos needed for the refinance appraisal and underwriting. If the house is in unincorporated Greenville County, the county permit records are included too, since appraisers and underwriters sometimes ask which office signed off on the work. The package is organized so the file moves through underwriting without repeated requests.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Greenville, SC | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Rental property renovation in Greenville, SC: rent-ready rehabs, turns and deferred maintenance for Upstate landlords and single-family portfolio owners.
rental-renovation.intro: Greenville's rental stock ranges from century-old mill houses to post-war ranches and suburban subdivisions, and each type ages in its own way. Genstone Construction renovates single-family rentals across Greenville County and the Upstate for individual landlords, funds, REITs and other portfolio owners. The work runs through vetted, licensed Upstate contractors, with one Genstone field manager responsible for each house. Photos and milestones keep you informed, and each payment follows finished work. For multi-property owners, we can set consistent specifications while still scoping each house for its era and construction. Our Upstate rental work covers acquisition rehabs on mill houses and ranches, quick turns on suburban houses in Mauldin and Simpsonville and catch-up work on portfolios that have gone several years without capital investment. Ice storms and summer heat both shape the scope.

sections.h2: Rental standards across Greenville's housing types
sections.body:
A Greenville rental portfolio might include a mill house in Judson or Brandon, a 1950s ranch in Berea and a 2000s house in Simpsonville. Same tenant pool, three very different repair lists. The mill house needs pier, framing and full systems work. The ranch needs HVAC, electrical and plumbing updates and crawlspace moisture correction. The Simpsonville house is mostly waiting on its original roof, heat pump and water heater to wear out.

Our portfolio specification locks in the things tenants see and maintenance techs replace, from flooring and paint colors to fixtures, appliances and hardware, so parts stay standard and quality stays even. Each property then gets a scope built around its age and construction. When a project is complete, we record system ages and equipment details in the property file, giving your property manager a real basis for capital planning instead of guessing when the next system will fail. Properties in unincorporated Greenville County are noted separately, since permit history lives with a different office.

Most Greenville rental calls trace back to a short list: HVAC struggling in summer heat or winter cold, frozen pipes during ice storms, moisture in crawlspaces and bathrooms, termites, and sewer backups in older houses with root-damaged laterals. A rental renovation that addresses those causes pays back every year.

We size heat pumps correctly and seal ductwork. Supply lines in crawlspaces and basements are insulated against freezing. Bath fans vent outdoors and tub surrounds are chosen for watertight joints. Under the floor, we lay vapor barriers and fix the drainage that feeds the moisture. Termite treatment with a renewable bond protects framing. Older sewer laterals are camera-inspected and repaired when needed. Inside, luxury vinyl plank, scrubbable paint and durable counters handle turnover. Those choices don't change a listing photo much, but they lower what the property costs to own. In the mill villages, insulating floors and walls during renovation does as much for tenant retention as any finish upgrade, because those houses were built without insulation and tenants feel it in both July and January. Heat pumps with properly sized auxiliary heat handle the Upstate's cold snaps without the no-heat calls that older systems produce.

Fast turns protect rental income. Genstone Construction handles make-ready work across the Greenville area, and our sister company Genstone Field Services supports portfolio owners with inspections, occupied maintenance, turns and code compliance. A Greenville turn usually covers paint, flooring fixes, a check of fixtures and appliances, cleaning and tenant-damage repairs.

Photos at move-out support your property manager's deposit decisions. When a turn reveals a larger issue, such as termite damage, a soft floor near a tub, a sloping floor that points to pier problems or a sewer backup, we document it and price it separately so you can decide whether to address it now or plan it for later. Payment follows each finished turn, and our workmanship warranty runs one year on the repairs, excluding tenant damage and normal wear. After an ice storm, we can walk a list of your Greenville rentals, document roof and tree damage with photos and prioritize the urgent items. Portfolio owners can also pre-approve standard turn pricing, so routine make-ready starts the day keys come back and only unusual findings wait for a decision.

faqs.q: Do you work with large rental owners in Greenville?
faqs.a: Yes. Our Upstate rental clients range from single-house owners to funds, REITs, servicers and banks. For portfolio owners in the Upstate, we standardize specifications, turn pricing and reporting across properties. Every property keeps its own scope, budget and file regardless. Owners whose houses are split between the city, unincorporated Greenville County and towns like Mauldin or Greer can use one specification and reporting format across all of them, and our field managers track which office permitted each job.

faqs.q: Can you prevent frozen pipes in Greenville rentals?
faqs.a: We insulate exposed supply lines in crawlspaces and basements, seal openings that let cold air in and recommend keeping heat on in vacant houses. Those steps reduce freeze risk during Upstate ice storms and cold snaps. For vacant properties, Genstone Field Services can also handle winterization. In mill houses and older ranches with open crawlspaces, closing foundation vents and adding skirting repairs often makes as much difference as pipe insulation.

faqs.q: Can you work on occupied Greenville rentals?
faqs.a: Most of it, yes. We routinely change out heat pumps, roofs, water heaters and windows with tenants living in the house, and Genstone Field Services covers occupied maintenance. Larger projects like kitchen remodels or pier and framing work are easier between leases. We coordinate access and notice through your property manager and protect tenant belongings. During summer, HVAC replacements in occupied Greenville rentals are scheduled quickly to limit how long tenants go without cooling.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Greenville, SC | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Duplex and small multifamily renovation in Greenville, SC: divided older houses, mill-area duplexes and suburban fourplexes, phased around tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Greenville
multifamily-renovation.intro: Greenville's small multifamily properties are spread across the county rather than concentrated in one area. Some larger houses near downtown and in older neighborhoods were divided into apartments decades ago, duplexes sit among single-family houses in and around the mill villages, and 1960s through 1980s duplexes and fourplexes serve working renters in Berea, Taylors, Mauldin and other suburbs. Genstone Construction renovates those properties for investors who need shared systems upgraded, units modernized, tenants managed during construction and permits handled correctly. One field manager runs the licensed trades on each building, and payments follow finished stages. Termite damage, crawlspace moisture and freeze protection come up in nearly every Upstate building we evaluate, so they're priced from the beginning.

sections.body:
Some larger houses near downtown, along North Main and in older neighborhoods were converted to apartments, often with limited fire separation and shared systems. Expect to find one electrical service feeding several subpanels, plumbing stacks that serve more than one apartment, back stairs added for upstairs tenants and alarms well short of today's requirements. Some conversions were never approved, so confirming the legal unit count with the city or county before purchase is essential.

Renovation starts with life safety and shared systems: separate HVAC for each unit, upgraded electrical service with separate panels and meters, fire-rated separation between units, interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and code-compliant egress. In the preservation overlay districts, exterior changes like new stairs or windows need design review. Apartments are then finished one by one, with the first completed unit setting the standard. Because these houses often sit on sloping lots, a lower-level unit may also need drainage and moisture work before it can be rented reliably.

The duplexes and fourplexes built across Berea, Taylors, Mauldin, Wade Hampton and other suburban areas from the 1960s through the 1980s were designed as multifamily from the start. They tend to have simple, repeated floor plans, slab or crawlspace foundations and shared roofs, with original systems that are failing together: HVAC, water heaters, early electrical panels, windows and, in some 1980s buildings, polybutylene supply lines.

Identical plans work in your favor. Scope one unit and you've scoped them all, and cabinets, flooring and fixtures can be bought for the whole building. Roofs, water and sewer lines, drainage and exterior repairs are handled first, then units are finished together in an empty building or one by one around tenants. Many of these buildings sit in unincorporated Greenville County or in suburban towns, so we confirm the permitting jurisdiction at the start. Buildings near major employers along the Interstate 85 corridor tend to fill quickly once renovated.

Many small multifamily properties around Greenville sell with tenants in place. Shared systems go first, with every shutoff arranged through your property manager and kept as short as possible. Apartments are renovated as tenants leave, while dust, noise, fire separation and alarms are managed for the people still living next door.

Seasonal planning matters in the Upstate. Roofing and major exterior work are scheduled for spring and fall when possible, and winter projects in occupied buildings require care to keep heat and water running during ice storms and cold snaps. Buildings near Furman or Bob Jones University may see leases end together, which creates windows for heavier interior work. Draws follow completed units, so capital tracks progress, and your field manager documents each phase with photos. If a building is in unincorporated Greenville County, we confirm whether county inspections can be scheduled around tenant availability. In older buildings with shared crawlspaces, freeze protection for supply lines serving occupied units is installed before winter, so a cold snap doesn't leave every tenant without water.

faqs.q: How do I confirm a Greenville duplex is legal?
faqs.a: Check with the City of Greenville or Greenville County, depending on the property's location, to confirm the legal unit count and zoning before purchase. Some conversions were never approved. We can help identify the jurisdiction during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review. If units were added without approval, the building may need to go through approval or be reduced in unit count, which changes the investment entirely. Knowing that before you buy is far cheaper than finding out during permitting.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Greenville fourplex with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. We schedule shared work like roofing or water service replacement with advance notice, then renovate units as they become vacant or on a schedule coordinated with tenants. Because tenant-occupied work runs longer, the plan and draws are sized for it at the start. Your property manager receives a schedule and notice for every shutoff, and fire separation and smoke alarms stay in service for occupied units the whole time. During winter, we make sure heat and water stay on for occupied units.

faqs.q: Can I use FHA 203(k) to buy a Greenville duplex?
faqs.a: Yes. Owner-occupants can use a 203(k) on buildings of up to four units. Genstone, as a certified 203(k) contractor, prepares the bid and draw paperwork the lender will ask for. That makes it an option for owner-occupant investors buying an older Greenville duplex near downtown or in the suburbs, living in one unit while rent from the others helps carry the mortgage. Your lender can confirm current eligibility and program limits, and we can price the renovation before you commit.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Greenville, SC | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Greenville, SC: bids, consultant coordination and draws for Limited and Standard loans on mill houses and Upstate ranches.
fha-203k.intro: As Greenville's popularity has grown, renovated houses near downtown and the Swamp Rabbit Trail have moved beyond many buyers' budgets. The FHA 203(k) loan offers another path: buy an unrenovated mill house or ranch and finance the repairs together with the purchase. Genstone's FHA 203(k) contractor certification lets us bid these loans directly. Buyers, their agents, renovation lenders and HUD consultants get the itemized bid and draw paperwork from us, and the renovation itself is run by a Genstone field manager with licensed Upstate trades. Many of the Greenville houses that fit most often need structural, termite or systems work that keeps them from qualifying for a standard FHA loan. Mill villages near the Swamp Rabbit Trail are a common fit.

sections.body:
Upstate buyers with non-structural needs can use the Limited 203(k), which covers up to $75,000 of work without a HUD consultant. For many Greenville ranches, that covers a roof, HVAC replacement, an electrical panel upgrade, a PEX repipe, windows, kitchen and bath updates, flooring and lead-safe paint work. Minor termite repairs may also fit.

Anything structural, or simply larger, belongs in the Standard 203(k), with its $5,000 minimum repair amount and a HUD consultant who writes the scope and inspects each draw. In Greenville, Standard loans are common on mill houses that need pier rebuilding and floor framing work, older houses with significant termite damage, houses with failing basement walls on hillside lots and projects that reconfigure the floor plan or add a bathroom. Our free review tells you which version the house probably needs before the lender sets up the loan. Lead-safe practices apply to almost every Greenville house of that era, and we include them in the bid wherever painted surfaces will be disturbed.

Greenville's mill houses are natural 203(k) candidates for buyers who want to live near downtown and the Swamp Rabbit Trail but can't afford a finished renovation. A typical mill house 203(k) includes pier and floor framing repair, termite treatment and damage repair, complete rewiring and replumbing, insulation, a new HVAC system and, often, a second bathroom. That usually makes it a Standard 203(k).

Because many mill villages sit in unincorporated Greenville County, permits go through the county rather than the city, and we confirm the jurisdiction at the start. Hidden damage is common once floors and walls are opened, so the contingency reserve matters. We document findings with photos and submit change orders through the lender and consultant before proceeding. Buyers see progress through the field manager's photos and milestones and approve the final work before the last payment. For many buyers, a 203(k) on a mill house is the most realistic way to own near the trail, since finished renovations on the same streets often sell beyond first-time buyer budgets.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws in Greenville County
sections.body:
The lender wants a line-item bid from a licensed contractor, and on Standard loans that bid has to agree with the consultant's write-up. Genstone's estimators prepare detailed bids with labor and materials by line item and coordinate with the HUD consultant to resolve differences before underwriting.

We submit each draw as its stage is finished, and on Standard loans nothing is paid until the consultant has inspected. The City of Greenville, Greenville County or the appropriate town issues permits and performs code inspections, and the final inspection must be complete before the last draw. We manage permits, design review where needed, inspections, the CL-100 and lien waivers from every trade. Final payment follows the homeowner's approval. If the house sits in one of the city's preservation overlay districts, design review for exterior work is filed early so it doesn't delay the final draw. Termite treatment and the CL-100 are coordinated at the start of the project, since lenders typically want that report before the loan closes out. Buyers and agents can follow progress through the field manager's photos and milestones.

faqs.q: Which Greenville houses fit the 203(k) program?
faqs.a: You want a price that leaves room for the work and a finished value that covers the entire loan. In Greenville, that often means unrenovated mill houses, ranches in Berea, Taylors and Wade Hampton and older houses in neighborhoods like Nicholtown and Southernside. Owner-occupied duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes qualify too. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tells buyers and agents whether a specific Greenville address is a realistic candidate.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover pier and floor repairs?
faqs.a: They can, but only under the Standard 203(k). Pier rebuilding and floor framing repair are structural work, which the Limited program doesn't cover. That version brings in a HUD consultant and sets a $5,000 minimum repair amount. Greenville mill houses commonly need this kind of work, so we assess piers, beams and joists during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review. That way the buyer and lender choose the correct program from the start, and the structural budget reflects what is actually under the house rather than an allowance.

faqs.q: Do Greenville 203(k) buyers need to move out during renovation?
faqs.a: On most projects, yes, because kitchens, baths or major systems are out of service. Some lenders allow mortgage payments for part of the renovation period to be included in the loan. We provide a realistic schedule with the bid. Smaller Limited projects that keep the existing heat and air running sometimes allow the buyer to move in sooner. If the buyer's current lease ends on a fixed date, tell us at the start so the schedule we submit to the lender accounts for it.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Greenville, SC | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned renovation in Greenville, SC for servicers, banks, funds and GSEs: securing, repairing and documenting vacant Upstate properties.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Greenville
reo-renovation.intro: Vacant houses in the Upstate face both summer humidity and winter ice, and older Greenville properties add pier, termite and systems problems that worsen without attention. Our REO clients are mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and Government-Sponsored Enterprises count Genstone among their preferred contractors. Across Greenville County, we coordinate vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors managed by a Genstone field manager who produces the documentation asset managers require: itemized bids, photo documentation, permit records, inspection results and lien waivers from every trade. The REO experience of our executive team is reflected in how Greenville properties are secured, scoped and reported. Many Greenville REO properties sit in unincorporated county areas, so we confirm the permitting and code enforcement jurisdiction on the first visit.

sections.body:
In summer, humidity builds inside vacant Greenville houses with the HVAC off, and mold spreads on drywall, cabinets and ceilings. Crawlspaces collect moisture, floors cup and termites continue damaging framing. In winter, ice storms bring limbs down on roofs no one is watching, and supply lines in crawlspaces and basements can freeze if the house wasn't winterized properly.

Theft and vandalism are also common, with HVAC condensers, copper and appliances as targets and broken windows inviting trespassers. Overgrown yards and debris draw complaints. Older mill houses may have settling piers that worsen without maintenance. Securing the house, stopping water and treating termites come first on an Upstate REO, followed by mold removal, replacement of stolen or failed systems and the repairs a buyer's lender will require. Our first visit on a Greenville REO focuses on stopping further loss: securing openings, clearing gutters, diverting water, requesting power for dehumidification where the client allows it and photographing everything so the asset manager knows the true starting condition. In winter, we also confirm the plumbing is drained or heated.

sections.h2: Permits and code enforcement for Greenville REO
sections.body:
Code enforcement for overgrown lots, debris and unsafe structures is handled by the City of Greenville inside city limits and by Greenville County in unincorporated areas. Open code cases can complicate a sale, so we address cited violations first, document corrections with photos and coordinate re-inspection.

Renovation permits go through the City of Greenville, Greenville County or the appropriate town, and properties in preservation overlay districts need design review for exterior changes. For REO clients we keep permit records, inspection results, the CL-100 and lien waivers in the property file so they're available to buyers, title and lenders. Genstone Field Services can handle preservation, winterization, inspections and code compliance alongside renovation, keeping one consistent record. Several mill villages straddle city and county lines, so the jurisdiction is confirmed before any filing. That continuity in the record matters when a buyer's lender or attorney asks whether a cited violation was corrected, and when the property changes hands among investors later.

sections.h2: Choosing the right REO scope in Greenville
sections.body:
The repair budget for a Greenville REO should follow its likely buyer. In North Main, Augusta Road, the renovated mill villages and other neighborhoods with strong owner-occupant demand, buyers compare listings with renovated houses, so a fuller renovation can significantly improve recovery. In areas with more investor buyers, a repair-to-market scope that brings the house to financeable condition is often the better choice.

A repair-to-market scope typically includes a sound roof, working HVAC, functional plumbing and electrical, termite treatment and repair with a clean CL-100, mold remediation, safety items like handrails and smoke alarms and lead-safe paint correction on pre-1978 houses. We price both options when the choice isn't clear, with line items and photos in the client's required format. Near the Swamp Rabbit Trail, an unrenovated bank-owned mill house may also attract strong interest from investors who want to do their own work, which is worth weighing before committing to a full renovation. Each bid reflects the conditions documented at our walkthrough, including pier, termite and crawlspace findings that a drive-by valuation can't capture.

faqs.q: Does Genstone handle GSE-owned properties in Greenville?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone is on the preferred contractor list for Government-Sponsored Enterprises, and we also serve Upstate servicers, banks and other lenders. Bids follow each client's required format, and the property file carries photos, permits and every lien waiver. A designated field manager is the single point of contact for each Greenville-area address, from the first securing visit through the final listing photos, and the file notes whether the property sits in the city, the county or another town.

faqs.q: Can you winterize vacant Greenville properties?
faqs.a: Yes, through Genstone Field Services, our sister company for preservation, winterization, inspections and code compliance. Winterization matters in Greenville because ice storms and cold snaps can freeze supply lines in crawlspaces and basements. Older mill houses with open crawlspaces are especially exposed, so we also check for broken foundation vents and missing skirting that let cold air reach the pipes. With one organization doing both preservation and repairs, the record never has a gap.

faqs.q: How do you handle mold in a vacant Greenville house?
faqs.a: We identify the moisture source first, remove affected materials, correct the cause and document conditions before and after. If the growth is extensive, a licensed remediation firm does that portion under our management. In Greenville's humid summers, mold spreads quickly once the HVAC is off, so restoring power and running dehumidification early can limit the damage before remediation begins. The asset manager receives photos of the moisture source and the corrected condition.
